final_proof:
The proposed argument is not correct: replacing two equations by their sum loses information, and the asserted reduction for inequations is false in general. Here is a precise statement and proof in the usual setting.

Let \((K,\delta)\) be a differential field, and let \(R=K[D;\delta]\) be the ring of linear differential operators, where \(Da=aD+\delta(a)\). Let the unknown \(x\) range over any differential field extension of \(K\). For every finite family \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\in R\) and right-hand sides \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\), the conjunction
\[
  \bigwedge_{j=1}^n P_jx=f_j
\]
is equivalent to one linear differential equation \(Gx=h\), together with a conjunction containing no \(x\).

Indeed, \(R\) is a left principal ideal domain. (The usual cancellation of leading terms gives left division with remainder, since the leading coefficient of a nonzero operator is invertible in \(K\); the Euclidean algorithm then proves that every finitely generated left ideal is principal.) Hence
\[
  RP_1+\cdots+RP_n=RG
\]
for some \(G\in R\). Because \(G\) belongs to the left ideal on the left, there are \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\in R\) such that
\[
  G=\sum_{j=1}^nU_jP_j.
\]
Because every \(P_j\) belongs to \(RG\), there is an \(A_j\in R\) such that \(P_j=A_jG\). Put
\[
  h=\sum_{j=1}^nU_jf_j.
\]
Then
\[
 \boxed{
 \bigwedge_{j=1}^n P_jx=f_j
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 Gx=h\ \land\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^n f_j=A_jh.}
\]
For the forward implication, applying the operators \(U_j\) and adding gives \(Gx=h\); moreover, \(f_j=P_jx=A_jGx=A_jh\). Conversely, if the right-hand side holds, then \(P_jx=A_jGx=A_jh=f_j\) for every \(j\). The final conjunction contains no \(x\), as required. This also covers the case in which all \(P_j\) are zero by taking \(G=0\), \(h=0\), and putting the conditions \(f_j=0\) in the \(x\)-free conjunction.

By contrast, a finite conjunction of linear differential inequations cannot in general be replaced by one linear differential inequation and an \(x\)-free condition. Take the differential field \(K=\mathbb Q\) with the zero derivation and consider
\[
  x\ne0\quad\land\quad x\ne1.
\]
Suppose it were equivalent over \(K\) to \(Lx\ne g\land\psi\), where \(L\in K[D]\) and \(\psi\) contains no \(x\). The displayed conjunction is satisfiable (for example by \(x=2\)), so \(\psi\) must be true. Since the derivation on \(K\) is zero, if \(L=a_0+a_1D+\cdots+a_mD^m\), then \(Lx=a_0x\) for every \(x\in K\). If \(a_0\ne0\), the condition \(Lx\ne g\) excludes exactly one element of \(K\), whereas \(x\ne0\land x\ne1\) excludes two. If \(a_0=0\), it excludes either no elements or all elements. In every case this is a contradiction.

The valid general replacement is the single, usually nonlinear, differential inequation
\[
  \bigwedge_{j=1}^n(P_jx\ne g_j)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \prod_{j=1}^n(P_jx-g_j)\ne0,
\]
because a product in a field is nonzero exactly when every factor is nonzero. Introducing nonzero offsets \(a,b\) and adding does not repair the linear claim: as the question observes, they may cancel. Requiring positivity is unavailable in an arbitrary differential field and, even over an ordered field, would not give an equivalent reformulation of arbitrary inequations.
